Session 3: Workflow
:::

### How to set up a review process {style="color:#FDFEFE"}

::: {.subtle-light}
One agent gathers evidence and forms no opinion. A second agent critiques — without ever seeing the original document. Every finding traces back to a source. This is how you trust AI on something that matters.
:::

:::

## What we'll cover {background-color="#ffffff"}

:::: {.split-grid}

::: {.sg-col}
::: {.sg-head}
Part 1 · The idea
:::
::: {.sg-body}
• Recap: what an **agent** is<br>
• Two agents, two jobs — researcher & reviewer<br>
• Why separating them removes bias<br>
• Three rules: separate, trace, admit doubt<br>
• Why the process runs in this order<br>
• The shape of the review
:::
:::

::: {.sg-col .accent}
::: {.sg-head}
Part 2 · The live run
:::
::: {.sg-body}
• `/researcher` → the evidence briefing<br>
• The checkpoint — you fix the *evidence*<br>
• `/reviewer` → findings, ranked and rated<br>
• Trace a LOW rating back to its source<br>
• Change the evidence, re-run one step
:::
:::

to go faster, this one uses them to be more trustworthy. Don't explain how yet —

# Part 1 — The idea: separate the roles {background-color="#ffffff"}

## What's an agent, really? {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {.term-hero}
::: {.th-name}
Agent
:::
::: {.th-def}
A **fresh Claude** with its **own clean context**, given one role and one input.
It can't be swayed by a conversation it never saw.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-box .warn}
[Why "fresh" is the whole point]{.cb-label}
If the same Claude gathers the evidence *and* judges it, it tends to defend its
first impression. Splitting the work across two agents removes that bias by
design.
:::

::: {.notes}
Straight callback to Session 2 — same agents, new purpose. There we used them for
speed: ten files read in parallel. Here we use exactly one property, the clean
context, to buy independence instead. Say that out loud; it's the hinge of the
whole session.
:::

## Researcher vs. Reviewer {background-color="#ffffff"}

::::: {.mode-grid}

:::: {.mode-card .skills}
::: {.mode-icon}
🔍
:::
::: {.mode-title}
Researcher
:::
::: {.mode-desc}
Reads the strategy, the prior strategy, and the org context. Maps claims,
assumptions, commitments, gaps. **Forms no opinion.** Every line cites a source.
:::
::: {.mode-badge}
Evidence only
:::
::::

:::: {.mode-card .agents}
::: {.mode-icon}
⚖️
:::
::: {.mode-title}
Reviewer
:::
::: {.mode-desc}
Reads **only the briefing** — never the original. Applies a 5-lens critique,
rates confidence HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW, ranks findings by severity.
:::
::: {.mode-badge}
Judgment only
:::
::::

:::::

::: {.callout-box .warn}
[Separation is not optional]{.cb-label}
The researcher finishes *before* the reviewer starts. The reviewer works from
the evidence briefing, not the strategy — so it can't rationalise the document
into looking fine.
:::

::: {.notes}
The counter-intuitive bit is that the reviewer never reads the strategy. People
assume that makes the review weaker. It's the opposite: the reviewer can only
work from what the researcher could actually evidence, so a claim nobody could
source never reaches the judgment stage.
:::

## Three rules this session lives by {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {.steps}

::: {.step}
::: {.step-num}
1
:::
::: {.step-body}
**Separate the roles.** The researcher completes its work before the reviewer
sees anything.
:::
:::

::: {.step}
::: {.step-num}
2
:::
::: {.step-body}
**Every claim needs a trail.** Each finding traces to a specific source file and
passage. Untraceable claims are *removed*, not summarised.
:::
:::

::: {.step}
::: {.step-num}
3
:::
::: {.step-body}
**Uncertainty is explicit.** Weak, conflicting, or absent evidence is named as
such. Gaps are never filled with inference.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
These three lines are lifted verbatim from this demo's CLAUDE.md — worth showing
the file if the room is curious. The point to land: the discipline lives in
writing, not in anyone's memory, so it applies the same way every run.
:::

## Why does it run in this order? {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {style="font-size:0.6em; color:#5a5e66; margin-bottom:0.4em"}
Three rules, one specific order. Each choice below is what makes rule 1 —
"the researcher finishes before the reviewer starts" — actually
enforceable, not just aspirational.
:::

::::: {.term-grid}

::: {.term-card}
::: {.term-name}
Sequential, not parallel
:::
::: {.term-def}
Run both at once and the reviewer has nothing to review yet — and sharing
a context between them would smuggle the researcher's framing straight
into the judgment it's supposed to be independent of.
:::
:::

::: {.term-card}
::: {.term-name}
The reviewer never sees the source
:::
::: {.term-def}
Only the briefing, never the original strategy. That's what stops a claim
nobody could evidence from ever reaching the judgment stage — the reviewer
can't rationalize what it never read.
:::
:::

::: {.term-card}
::: {.term-name}
The checkpoint sits between the stages
:::
::: {.term-def}
It's the last moment where fixing the evidence is still cheap — before
it's locked into a critique. Move it later and you're editing conclusions
instead of facts.
:::
:::

::: {.term-card}
::: {.term-name}
The audit log is a byproduct, not an add-on
:::
::: {.term-def}
Every step already writes down what it read and why. Assembling that into
one trail costs nothing extra — and it's what turns "the AI said so" into
something defensible.
:::
:::

:::::

::: {.notes}
This is the "why" behind the pipeline diagram on the next slide — say it
before showing the diagram, not after, so the shape already makes sense by
the time they see the arrows. Each card maps to a real failure mode: skip
sequencing and you get a reviewer defending its own first impression; skip
the source-blocking and claims survive that nobody could ever back up;
move the checkpoint and you're relitigating a verdict instead of fixing a
fact; skip the audit log and there's no way to defend the review later.
:::

## The shape of the review {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {style="font-size:0.6em; color:#5a5e66; margin-bottom:0.3em"}
Two agents, one gate, four files on disk. Every arrow is a handoff you can open
and read.
:::

:::: {.pipeline-strip}
::: {.pipeline-card .input}
[Input]{.pc-step}

[Your documents]{.pc-title}

[strategy · prior · context]{.pc-meta}
:::

::: {.pipeline-link}
[/researcher]{.pc-cmd}

[→]{.pc-arrow}
:::

::: {.pipeline-card .handoff}
[Saved handoff]{.pc-step}

[research-briefing.md]{.pc-title}

[evidence, no opinion]{.pc-meta}
:::

::: {.pipeline-link}
[/reviewer]{.pc-cmd}

[→]{.pc-arrow}
:::

::: {.pipeline-card .handoff}
[Saved handoff]{.pc-step}

[review-findings.md]{.pc-title}

[ranked + rated]{.pc-meta}
:::

::: {.pipeline-link}
[assemble]{.pc-cmd}

[→]{.pc-arrow}
:::

::: {.pipeline-card .output}
[Final output]{.pc-step}

[report.docx]{.pc-title}

[+ audit-log.md]{.pc-meta}
:::
::::

::: {.callout-box .gate}
[The gate sits on the first arrow]{.cb-label}
Between the briefing and the reviewer, everything stops and waits for you. That
placement is deliberate — it's the last moment where correcting the evidence is
cheap.
:::

::: {.notes}
Compare to the Session 2 pipeline picture on purpose: same shape, different
reason. There the steps were split for re-runnability; here they're split so two
independent minds work on the same problem. Don't linger — the live run makes it
concrete.
:::

# Part 2 — Run the review {background-color="#ffffff"}

## The setup {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {.filetree}
03_multitudes/<br>
├── <span class="dir">sample-input/</span><br>
│   ├── strategy-2025.md          <span class="note"># the document under review</span><br>
│   ├── prior-strategy-2022.md    <span class="note"># for continuity & commitment checks</span><br>
│   └── org-context.md            <span class="note"># budget, staffing, constraints</span><br>
└── <span class="dir">output/</span>                       <span class="note"># briefing, findings, report, audit log</span>
:::

::: {.callout-box .tip}
[Add your own context]{.cb-label}
Drop in an evaluation report, a stakeholder map, or budget data — the researcher
classifies and uses it automatically. More evidence, same discipline.
:::

::: {.notes}
The third file is the one that does the work. A strategy reviewed on its own can
only be checked for internal logic; org-context.md is what lets the review say
"you have eight coaches and you need fourteen." Point at it and say so.
:::

## Step 1 — /researcher {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {.chat}
<span class="you">/researcher</span>
<span class="cc">Read strategy-2025.md · prior-strategy-2022.md · org-context.md</span>
<span class="cc">Mapped 9 strategic claims, 5 core assumptions</span>
<span class="cc">Checked 5 commitments from 2022 → 1 dropped with no explanation</span>
<span class="cc">Capacity: Priority 1 PARTIALLY · Priority 2 PARTIALLY (LOW) · Priority 3 NO</span>
<span class="muted">Flagged 6 information gaps → saved output/research-briefing.md</span>
:::

::: {.callout-box .tip}
[Open the briefing before you go on]{.cb-label}
This is the teaching beat: read `research-briefing.md` together. Discuss what the
researcher *found* before the reviewer is allowed to judge it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Not one word of judgment in that output — it says Priority 3 is "NO" on capacity
because the file says $800K expires in July with nothing secured. That's a fact,
not a verdict. Open Section 3 of the briefing and show that each line ends in a
source. Then say: the reviewer gets this and nothing else.
:::

## The human checkpoint {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {.chat}
<span class="muted">━━━ CHECKPOINT — before the Reviewer proceeds ━━━</span>
<span class="cc">The researcher mapped: 9 claims · 5 assumptions · 5 prior commitments · 6 gaps</span>
<span class="cc">Full briefing: output/research-briefing.md</span>
<span class="cc">Anything to add or correct? Type "continue" to proceed.</span>
<span class="you">Add the 2024 evaluation report to the evidence, then continue.</span>
:::

::: {.callout-box .gate}
[You can change the evidence — not the verdict]{.cb-label}
The gate lets you correct or enrich the briefing. You never tell the reviewer
what to conclude. That stays the agent's call, from the evidence.
:::

::: {.notes}
Say the distinction in plain words, because it's the one people reach for first:
"add the board minutes, they cover the funding gap" is fair game. "Go easier on
Priority 3" is not — that's you writing the finding and laundering it through the
agent. Adding evidence keeps the trail honest; steering the conclusion breaks it.
:::

## The five lenses {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#5a5e66; margin-bottom:0.2em"}
The reviewer works through all five, in order, against the briefing only.
:::

::: {.steps style="font-size:0.86em"}

::: {.step}
::: {.step-num}
1
:::
::: {.step-body}
**Internal consistency** — do the priorities pull the same way? Does the money
follow the stated ranking?
:::
:::

::: {.step}
::: {.step-num}
2
:::
::: {.step-body}
**Evidence quality** — is each major claim supported? Are the metrics measurable
with the systems that exist?
:::
:::

::: {.step}
::: {.step-num}
3
:::
::: {.step-body}
**Feasibility** — given the capacity assessment, which priorities can actually be
delivered as written?
:::
:::

::: {.step}
::: {.step-num}
4
:::
::: {.step-body}
**Continuity & accountability** — were prior commitments met, dropped, or quietly
abandoned?
:::
:::

::: {.step}
::: {.step-num}
5
:::
::: {.step-body}
**Blind spots** — what would an outside reader expect to see here that simply
isn't mentioned?
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Lens 1 is the one that catches the classic failure — "Priority 3 is critical" next
to a budget line of $0. Lens 5 is the hardest for a human reviewer to do honestly,
because noticing an absence means knowing what should have been there. Mention
that these five live in skills/reviewer.md and can be edited to fit your own
review framework.
:::

## Step 2 — /reviewer {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {.chat}
<span class="you">/reviewer</span>
<span class="cc">Read output/research-briefing.md (not the original strategy)</span>
<span class="cc">🔴 Critical: $800K expires July 2026, no replacement secured        [HIGH]</span>
<span class="cc">🔴 Critical: Priority 3 has $0 budget and 20% of one person's time  [HIGH]</span>
<span class="cc">🟡 Moderate: guide has no staff — $90K budgeted, $12K spent         [HIGH]</span>
<span class="cc">🟢 Minor:   2022 leadership programme dropped, never explained      [MEDIUM]</span>
<span class="muted">8 findings (3 · 3 · 2) + 4 strengths → saved output/review-findings.md</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Two things to point out. First, severity and confidence are different axes — the
moderate finding there is rated HIGH confidence, because the budget numbers are
exact. A small problem you're certain of is not a big problem you're guessing at.
Second, it found four strengths. A reviewer that only ever finds fault is just as
useless as one that never does.
:::

## Tracing a confidence rating {background-color="#ffffff"}

:::: {.split-grid}

::: {.sg-col .accent}
::: {.sg-head}
The finding
:::
::: {.sg-body}
🟢 *The strategy calls the funder's shift to larger, fewer grants an
"opportunity" — without examining whether CLI is positioned to win one.*<br>
**Confidence: LOW**
:::
:::

::: {.sg-col}
::: {.sg-head}
Why LOW — trace it
:::
::: {.sg-body}
The underlying fact is solid: the strategy says the funder is consolidating. But
whether that's an opportunity or a threat is a **judgment about framing**, and no
source file settles it — gap #3 notes there's no record of CLI ever discussing it
with the funder. Inference from an absence, so: LOW.
:::
:::

::::

::: {.callout-box .warn}
[The teaching question]{.cb-label}
"Why does it say LOW here?" Trace it back live. LOW isn't weakness — it's the
system being honest that the evidence is thin.
:::

::: {.notes}
Put this next to Finding 1 for contrast: that one is HIGH because two files give
the same dollar amount and the same date. Same reviewer, same run, different
confidence — because the evidence underneath is genuinely different. Ask the room
which of the two they'd take to a board meeting. Both, but not in the same tone.
:::

## Step 3 — /strategy-review {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#5a5e66; margin-bottom:0.3em"}
Orchestrates both agents in sequence, then assembles the formatted report —
research briefing, findings, overall assessment, and the audit log as an appendix.
:::

::: {.chat}
<span class="you">/strategy-review</span>
<span class="muted">▸ Researcher agent … → research-briefing.md</span>
<span class="muted">▸ CHECKPOINT (waits for you)</span>
<span class="muted">▸ Reviewer agent … → review-findings.md</span>
<span class="cc">✓ output/strategy-review-report.docx</span>
<span class="cc">✓ output/audit-log.md — every action, source, and decision</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Worth naming: the one-command version still stops at the checkpoint. Automating
the pipeline didn't automate away the human — that's the difference between a
workflow and a black box.
:::

## Change the evidence, re-run {background-color="#ffffff"}

:::: {.split-grid}

::: {.sg-col}
::: {.sg-head}
The slow way
:::
::: {.sg-body}
A colleague sends the 2024 evaluation report the morning after. Re-read every
file, re-do the whole critique, rebuild the report from scratch.
:::
:::

::: {.sg-col .accent}
::: {.sg-head}
The pipeline way
:::
::: {.sg-body}
Drop it into `sample-input/`, re-run <span class="cmd">/researcher</span> only.
The briefing changes — maybe a gap closes, maybe a claim finally has evidence.
Then let the reviewer see the new briefing.
:::
:::

::::

::: {.callout-box .tip}
[Watch a finding move]{.cb-label}
This is the demo that makes separation click. New evidence changes the briefing;
the changed briefing changes the finding. Nobody argued with the reviewer — the
evidence underneath it moved.
:::

::: {.notes}
The headline demo of the session. Do it live if there's time: add a file, re-run
just the researcher, and show gap #3 closing. Then re-run the reviewer and watch
that LOW finding either firm up or disappear. It's the clearest possible proof
that the verdict is downstream of the evidence rather than of the prompt.
:::

## The audit log is the trust story {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {.chat}
<span class="muted">[RESEARCHER] Read: strategy-2025.md (~2,400 words)</span>
<span class="muted">[RESEARCHER] Identified 9 strategic claims</span>
<span class="muted">[RESEARCHER] Flagged 6 information gaps</span>
<span class="muted">── HUMAN CHECKPOINT ── User reviewed briefing and typed: continue</span>
<span class="muted">[REVIEWER]   Applied Lens 3: Feasibility</span>
<span class="muted">[REVIEWER]   Identified 8 findings (3 critical, 3 moderate, 2 minor)</span>
:::

::: {.callout-box .tip}
[Why it matters at high stakes]{.cb-label}
Anyone can re-trace what was read, what was concluded, and why. That's the
difference between "the AI said so" and a defensible review.
:::

::: {.notes}
Note the checkpoint line sits in the log too — the human decision is on the record
alongside the machine ones. If someone challenges the review in six months, this
file is the answer. Close the session here if you're short on time; it's the
strongest ending.
:::

## What you just saw {background-color="var(--slide-dark-bg)"}

::: {.center-all style="color:#FDFEFE"}

::: {.eyebrow}
Key concept
:::

### Separating roles produces more reliable, less biased analysis.

::: {.subtle-light}
A researcher that only gathers, a reviewer that only judges, every claim traced
to a source, and uncertainty stated out loud. The audit log lets a human stand
behind the result.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The payoff for the whole session. One sentence: you didn't get a better answer by
writing a better prompt, you got one by designing who was allowed to know what.
:::

## Your turn {background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {style="font-size:0.62em; color:var(--brand-dark); margin-bottom:0.4em"}
Point the pipeline at a real strategy or plan:
:::

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.6em; margin-top:0.5em"}
- Add a context file, re-run `/researcher` only — watch a gap close.
- "Summarise the critical findings for the board in one page."
- "Draft a response memo addressing the top 3 concerns."
- "Show me every finding rated LOW, and what evidence would raise it."
:::

::: {.notes}
The last prompt is the best one to leave them with — asking what would raise a
rating turns the review into a to-do list. Ten minutes on their own document is
where this sticks.
:::
